questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish a risk from an assumption?
options: A risk only applies to technical systems, while an assumption only applies to people
They are the same thing, just phrased differently
A risk is a possible future event that would be bad if it happened; an assumption is a belief the design is quietly standing on without stakeholder confirmation
An assumption is always more severe than any risk
questions.explain: A risk is an event with a probability and an impact (the migration takes longer than planned); an assumption is a belief the design depends on without explicit confirmation (leadership values unified reporting enough to accept the cost) — different kinds of statement, even though both represent uncertainty.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a low-likelihood, high-impact risk can deserve disproportionate design attention?
options: Because low-likelihood risks should always be ignored
Because impact is always the same for every risk in a register
Because likelihood doesn't matter once a risk is identified
Because the cost of being wrong is so large that it outweighs the low probability, unlike a high-likelihood but low-impact risk that just needs a documented fallback
questions.explain: Scoring both likelihood and impact separately is what surfaces risks like Veltrix's usage-pipeline failure: unlikely, but catastrophic enough in impact to justify real design attention well beyond what a quick probability estimate alone would suggest.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue an unstated assumption can be worse than a stated risk, even a serious one?
options: A stated risk is visible and can be challenged or mitigated; an unstated assumption is invisible until it breaks, often producing a failure nobody anticipated
Stated risks are never actually true
Unstated assumptions are always false
Assumptions cannot be written down, by definition
questions.explain: A reviewer can push back on, mitigate, or knowingly accept a stated risk. An assumption that's never written down can't be challenged at all — it just sits underneath the design until it turns out to be wrong, often producing a slow, hard-to-diagnose failure rather than a clean one.

questions.q: What four columns does this lesson say a usable risk-and-assumptions register needs per entry?
options: Only a description and a due date
The statement (labeled risk or assumption), likelihood/confidence, impact if wrong, and a mitigation or validation step
The architect's name, the date, a severity emoji, and a status color
A cost estimate and nothing else
questions.explain: A finished register entry states what it is (risk or assumption), scores likelihood (for risks) or confidence (for assumptions), states the impact if wrong, and names a concrete mitigation or validation step — without that last column, it's just a documented worry with no next action.

questions.q: In the Ferro consolidation example, what does the lesson identify as a silently-held, unstated assumption that could produce a slow, hard-to-diagnose failure if wrong?
options: That no sharing rules would ever be needed after consolidation
That Salesforce would refuse to support three business units in one org
That each unit's sales teams would tolerate a slower, heavier Opportunity process in exchange for unified reporting
That Ferro's customers would never buy from more than one unit
questions.explain: This assumption, if wrong, doesn't fail cleanly — it produces reps quietly working around the new process and data quality degrading over time, exactly the kind of invisible failure mode this lesson says an unstated assumption is prone to causing.
